subject: calculus
title: Limits
summary: What a limit is and how to find one: one-sided and infinite limits, limits at infinity, limit laws, the squeeze theorem, and continuity with the intermediate value theorem.

concepts.name: Limit of a function
concepts.summary: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a is the value f(x) gets close to when x gets close to a, whether or not f(a) exists.

elements.name: Approaching a point is not reaching it

explain.text: The limit of f(x) as x approaches a is the value that f(x) gets arbitrarily close to as x gets close to a, with x not equal to a. Only the values near a matter, so f(a) can be missing or different from the limit. Picture a graph with a hole at x = 2 and a single point off the hole at (2, 5): the limit is the height of the hole, 4 if the curve is y = x + 2. If f is a polynomial or another continuous function, the limit is found by plugging a in. When plugging in gives 0/0, factor and cancel first. The notation is lim as x → a of f(x).

concepts.name: One-sided limits
concepts.summary: A one-sided limit approaches a from only one side: from the right, written x → a⁺, or from the left, written x → a⁻.

explain.text: A one-sided limit looks at the values of f(x) from only one side of a. The right-hand limit, written x → a⁺, uses x values bigger than a. The left-hand limit, written x → a⁻, uses x values smaller than a. Picture a staircase: standing at the edge of one step, the height reached from the right and the height reached from the left can differ. The two-sided limit exists only when both one-sided limits exist and are equal, and then it is their common value. If they differ, the function has a jump at a.

concepts.name: Limit laws
concepts.summary: The limit laws say that the limit of a sum, product, quotient or power can be found from the limits of its parts, when those limits exist.

explain.text: The limit laws let you find the limit of a combined function from the limits of its parts. If the limit of f and the limit of g both exist at a, then the limit of f plus g is the sum of the two limits, and the same holds for differences, products and constant multiples. The quotient law works when the limit of g is not zero. For a power or a root, you can take the power or root of the limit, as long as the result is defined. These laws turn many limits into plain arithmetic, such as substituting a into a polynomial.

concepts.name: Infinite limits and vertical asymptotes
concepts.summary: An infinite limit means f(x) grows without bound as x approaches a, and a vertical asymptote is the line x = a near which this happens.

elements.name: Sign of a limit from each side

explain.text: Sometimes f(x) grows without bound as x approaches a. Writing the limit of f(x) as x → a equals ∞ means that f(x) gets larger than any number you choose, once x is close enough to a but not equal to a. The line x = a is then a vertical asymptote. An infinite limit is not a number, so the two-sided limit does not exist as a real number. For f(x) = 1/x, the function is large and positive just to the right of 0 and large and negative just to the left, so the two one-sided limits at 0 are ∞ and −∞.

concepts.name: Limits at infinity and horizontal asymptotes
aliases: limit as x goes to infinity
concepts.summary: A limit at infinity describes what f(x) approaches as x grows without bound, and a horizontal asymptote is the horizontal line the graph approaches that way.

explain.text: A limit at infinity asks what f(x) approaches as x grows without bound, written x → ∞, or as x decreases without bound, written x → −∞. For example, 1/x approaches 0 as x grows, so the line y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote. For a rational function, divide the top and bottom by the highest power of x in the denominator. Then every term with x in the denominator goes to 0. If the numerator has a higher degree than the denominator, the function grows without bound and has no horizontal asymptote.

concepts.name: Squeeze theorem
concepts.summary: If g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a, and g and h both have the same limit L at a, then f also has limit L at a.

elements.name: Bounded function times a function going to zero
The limit of sin x / x at 0

explain.text: The squeeze theorem handles a function that is trapped between two simpler functions. If g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) for x near a, and g and h both approach the same limit L as x approaches a, then f must also approach L. Picture f as a filling pressed between two slices of bread. It is useful when f is hard to evaluate directly, such as x² times sin(1/x). Because −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1 gives simple bounds, the squeeze can finish the job. The bounds need to hold only near a, not at a itself.

concepts.name: Continuity
concepts.summary: A function is continuous at a when f(a) is defined, its limit at a exists, and the two are equal, so its graph has no break at that point.

elements.name: Polynomials and rational functions are continuous

explain.text: A function f is continuous at a when three things hold: f(a) is defined, the limit of f(x) as x approaches a exists, and that limit equals f(a). If any one fails, the graph has a break at a. Polynomials are continuous everywhere, and rational functions are continuous everywhere they are defined. A function is continuous on an interval if it is continuous at every point of the interval. The break may be a hole, a jump, or an infinite gap, depending on which condition fails.

concepts.name: Intermediate value theorem
concepts.summary: If f is continuous on a closed interval [a, b], then f takes every value between f(a) and f(b), so it has a solution wherever its values change sign.

elements.name: A sign change gives a root

explain.text: The intermediate value theorem says that a function continuous on a closed interval [a, b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b). A typical use is finding a root. If f(a) is negative and f(b) is positive, then f must equal 0 somewhere between a and b. The theorem guarantees that such a point exists, but it does not say how many there are or how to find it exactly. Picture a continuous curve that starts below a horizontal line and ends above it: it must cross the line. Continuity on the whole interval is essential.

items.prompt: What is the limit of x² + 1 as x approaches 2?
items.explanation: x² + 1 is a polynomial, so the limit is found by substitution: 2² + 1 = 5. The tempting answer 4 squares 2 but drops the +1. The answer 3 uses 2 + 1 and forgets the square.

items.prompt: Which statement about the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is true?
choices: It depends only on values of f near a, not on the value at a itself
It is undefined whenever f(a) is undefined
It is the largest value f takes anywhere
items.explanation: The limit looks at values of f(x) for x near a but not equal to a, so f(a) can be missing or different. The first option is the common mistake. The third is wrong because a hole has a limit even though f(a) is undefined.

items.prompt: What is the limit of (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x approaches 2?
items.explanation: Substitution gives 0/0. Factor the numerator as (x − 2)(x + 2), cancel the common factor for x ≠ 2, and get x + 2, which tends to 4. The answer 0 treats 0/0 as 0, and 'Undefined' confuses the value at 2 with the limit.

items.prompt: What is the limit of (x² − 1)/(x + 1) as x approaches −1?
items.explanation: Factor x² − 1 as (x − 1)(x + 1) and cancel x + 1 for x ≠ −1 to get x − 1, which tends to −2 at −1. The answer 2 drops the sign. The answer 0 assumes the value is zero because the numerator vanishes, which is not how limits work.

items.prompt: In the definition saying the limit of f(x) as x approaches a is L, what does δ control?
choices: How close f(x) must be to L
How close x must be to a
items.explanation: In the epsilon-delta definition, ε sets how close f(x) must be to L, and δ is the matching distance from a that guarantees it. Choosing the first option swaps δ and ε.

items.prompt: Which best describes a removable discontinuity at x = a?
choices: The function jumps to a different value on each side of a
The function grows without bound as x approaches a
The limit at a exists, but f(a) is undefined or differs from it
The function oscillates forever near a
items.explanation: Both sides approach the same limit L, so redefining f(a) = L removes the gap. A jump has different one-sided limits, infinite growth is an infinite limit, and oscillation has no limit at all.

items.prompt: Let f(x) = x² for x ≠ 3, and f(3) = 10. What are the limit of f(x) as x approaches 3 and the value of f(3)?
items.explanation: The limit uses x near 3 with x ≠ 3, where f(x) = x² tends to 9. The value f(3) = 10 is set separately and does not change the limit. The first option swaps the two values.

items.prompt: Put the steps for finding the limit of (x² − 4)/(x − 2) as x approaches 2, in order.
steps: Try direct substitution and see that it gives 0/0
Cancel the common factor x − 2, which is allowed because x ≠ 2
items.explanation: Substitution comes first to reveal the 0/0 form. Factoring must come before cancelling, and the final substitution is valid only after the common factor is removed.

items.prompt: What does the limit of f(x) as x → a⁺ mean?
choices: x approaches a from values greater than a
x approaches a from values less than a
x is exactly equal to a
items.explanation: The superscript plus means x comes in from the right, through values larger than a. The minus version uses values smaller than a. The last option swaps x and f(x).

items.prompt: The left-hand limit at 3 is 5, and the right-hand limit at 3 is also 5. What is the two-sided limit at 3?
items.explanation: When both one-sided limits exist and are equal, the two-sided limit exists and equals their common value. The answer 3 confuses the point being approached with the limit value.

items.prompt: Let f(x) = 1 for x < 0 and f(x) = 4 for x ≥ 0. What is the right-hand limit of f at 0?
items.explanation: For x just above 0, f(x) is 4, so the right-hand limit is 4. The value 1 is the left-hand limit, which comes from the other side.

items.prompt: Using the same f (1 for x < 0 and 4 for x ≥ 0), what is the two-sided limit at 0?
items.explanation: The left-hand limit is 1 and the right-hand limit is 4. They differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist, even though f(0) = 4 is defined.

items.prompt: What is the left-hand limit of |x|/x as x approaches 0?
items.explanation: For x < 0, |x| = −x, so |x|/x = −x/x = −1 for every negative x. The right-hand limit is 1, which is why the two-sided limit fails.

items.prompt: Which describes a jump discontinuity at a?
choices: Both one-sided limits exist but are different
The function is undefined at a
Both one-sided limits equal f(a) and each other
items.explanation: A jump has finite one-sided limits that differ. Infinite one-sided limits describe an infinite discontinuity, and a function undefined at a may still have a limit there.

items.prompt: Which is true of f(x) = (x − 1)/|x − 1| near x = 1?
choices: The right-hand limit is 1 and the left-hand limit is −1, so the limit does not exist
The limit at 1 is 1 because f is positive on the right
The limit at 1 is −1 because the left side dominates
items.explanation: For x > 1, |x − 1| = x − 1, so f(x) = 1. For x < 1, |x − 1| = −(x − 1), so f(x) = −1. The one-sided limits differ, so the two-sided limit does not exist.

items.prompt: Put the steps for deciding whether the two-sided limit at a exists, in order.
steps: Find the left-hand limit and the right-hand limit at a
If they are equal, that common value is the two-sided limit
items.explanation: Both one-sided limits must be found before they can be compared, and the common value is reported only after the comparison confirms they match.

items.prompt: What is the limit of 3x + 1 as x approaches 2?
items.explanation: The limit of 3x is 6 by the constant multiple law, and adding the limit of 1 gives 7. The answer 6 forgets the +1.

items.prompt: Which law says the limit of f(x) times g(x) is the product of the two limits, when both exist?
items.explanation: The product law multiplies the limits. The sum law adds them, and the quotient law divides them only when the denominator's limit is not zero.

items.prompt: What is the limit of (x + 5)/(x − 1) as x approaches 4?
items.explanation: The numerator tends to 9 and the denominator to 3, so the quotient tends to 9/3 = 3. The answer 9 ignores the denominator, and 'Undefined' wrongly assumes a zero denominator limit.

items.prompt: The quotient law for limits applies when which condition holds?
choices: The limit of the denominator is zero
The limit of the denominator is not zero
items.explanation: The quotient law can divide only when the limit of the denominator is nonzero. The other options are not conditions of the law.

items.prompt: What is the limit of √(x + 3) as x approaches 1?
items.explanation: The root law lets you take the square root of the limit: x + 3 tends to 4, and √4 = 2. The answer √3 forgets to add 1 first, and 4 forgets the square root.

items.prompt: The limit of f(x) at a is 5, and the limit of g(x) at a is 0. What can the laws say about the limit of f(x)/g(x)?
choices: The quotient law cannot be applied directly, so the limit needs more work
items.explanation: The quotient law needs a nonzero limit in the denominator, so it does not decide the answer. The limit might be infinite or might not exist; the laws alone cannot say which.

items.prompt: What is the limit of (2x² − x)/(x + 3) as x approaches −1?
items.explanation: The numerator tends to 2(1) − (−1) = 3 and the denominator to 2, so the limit is 3/2. The answer 2/3 inverts the fraction, and 3 forgets the denominator.

items.prompt: What does the statement that the limit of f(x) as x → a equals ∞ mean?
choices: f(x) gets arbitrarily large as x gets close to a
f(x) equals a for every x
items.explanation: f(x) grows beyond any bound for x near a, but not at a itself. ∞ is not a value of f, so the second option is wrong. The last option describes a missing point, not growth.

items.prompt: Which line is a vertical asymptote of f(x) = 1/(x − 4)?
items.explanation: The denominator is zero at x = 4, so f grows without bound there, and x = 4 is the vertical asymptote. y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote of this function, but the question asks for a vertical one.

items.prompt: What is the left-hand limit of 1/x as x approaches 0?
items.explanation: For negative x close to 0, 1/x is a large negative number, so the left-hand limit is −∞. The right-hand limit is ∞, which is why the two-sided limit fails.

items.prompt: What is the limit of 1/(x − 3)² as x approaches 3?
items.explanation: The square is positive on both sides of 3 and grows without bound, so the limit is ∞. The answer −∞ forgets the square is always positive, and 0 confuses the limit with the function's value far from 3.

items.prompt: When does the graph of f have a vertical asymptote at x = a?
choices: At least one one-sided limit at a is infinite or minus infinity
The limit at a is a finite number
items.explanation: A vertical asymptote needs a one-sided limit that is infinite. A zero at a, a finite limit, or continuity at a all rule that out.

items.prompt: What is the limit of (x + 1)/(x − 2)² as x approaches 2?
items.explanation: The numerator tends to 3 and the squared denominator tends to 0 from above, so the quotient grows without bound: ∞. The answer 3 uses the numerator alone, and −∞ wrongly assumes a negative sign.

items.prompt: What is the left-hand limit of x/(x − 1) as x approaches 1?
items.explanation: Just below 1, the numerator is about 1 and the denominator is a small negative number, so the quotient is a large negative number: −∞. The answer ∞ comes from looking at the right side instead.

items.prompt: What is the limit of 1/x as x approaches ∞?
items.explanation: As x grows without bound, 1/x shrinks toward 0, so y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote. The value 1 is what 1/x equals at x = 1, not its limit at infinity.

items.prompt: Which is a horizontal asymptote of f(x) = (3x + 2)/x?
items.explanation: Dividing top and bottom by x gives 3 + 2/x, which approaches 3, so y = 3 is the horizontal asymptote. x = 0 is a vertical asymptote, not a horizontal one.

items.prompt: What is the limit of (2x² + 1)/(x² − 5) as x approaches ∞?
items.explanation: Dividing top and bottom by x² gives (2 + 1/x²)/(1 − 5/x²), which tends to 2/1 = 2. The answer 1/2 inverts the ratio of the leading coefficients.

items.prompt: What is the limit of (x² + 1)/x as x approaches ∞?
items.explanation: The function equals x + 1/x, which grows without bound as x grows. It is positive, so the limit is ∞, not −∞.

items.prompt: What is the limit of 1/x² as x approaches −∞?
items.explanation: x² is positive and grows without bound as x decreases, so 1/x² shrinks to 0. The answer 1 treats x² as constant, and ∞ mistakes growth for the reciprocal.

items.prompt: Which condition is needed for a rational function to have a horizontal asymptote?
choices: The numerator has higher degree than the denominator
The numerator's degree is at most the denominator's degree
The function has a zero at x = 0
items.explanation: When the numerator's degree is at most the denominator's, the function settles to a finite value, so a horizontal asymptote exists. A higher numerator degree makes the function grow without bound instead.

items.prompt: What is the limit of (3x³ − 2x)/(x³ + 5) as x approaches ∞?
items.explanation: Dividing by x³ gives (3 − 2/x²)/(1 + 5/x³), which tends to 3/1 = 3. The −2 is a lower-order term and does not affect the limit.

items.prompt: Put the steps for finding the limit of (4x + 1)/(2x − 3) as x approaches ∞, in order.
steps: Divide the numerator and the denominator by x
Let x approach ∞, so each 1/x term goes to 0
items.explanation: Dividing by the highest power of x comes first. The simplified form then exposes terms that shrink to zero, and only after that can the limit be read off.

items.prompt: In the squeeze theorem, where must g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) hold?
choices: For x near a, though not necessarily at a itself
items.explanation: The bounds only need to hold near a, and f need not equal either bound at a. Requiring the inequality for all real x is stronger than the theorem needs.

items.prompt: If g(x) ≤ f(x) ≤ h(x) near a, and both g and h have limit 4 at a, what is the limit of f at a?
items.explanation: The squeeze theorem forces f into the same limit as the two bounds. Saying 'cannot be determined' forgets that the theorem applies once the bounds share a limit.

items.prompt: What is the limit of x² · sin(1/x) as x approaches 0?
items.explanation: Since −1 ≤ sin(1/x) ≤ 1, multiplying by x² ≥ 0 gives −x² ≤ x² · sin(1/x) ≤ x², and both bounds tend to 0. The answer 'Does not exist' ignores the squeeze.

items.prompt: For x in (0, π/2), which pair of bounds is used to squeeze sin x / x toward 1?
items.explanation: For small positive x, cos x ≤ sin x / x ≤ 1. Both bounds tend to 1 as x approaches 0, so sin x / x does too. The bounds −1 and 1 are too far apart to give a limit.

items.prompt: Why can the squeeze theorem not show that the limit of sin(1/x) as x approaches 0 exists?
choices: No two bounds with equal limits exist, because sin(1/x) keeps oscillating between −1 and 1 near 0
items.explanation: Bounds such as −1 and 1 do not share a limit, and sin(1/x) takes every value between −1 and 1 in every interval around 0. The sine function is bounded, so the first option is false.

items.prompt: Which argument shows that the limit of sin(x)/x as x approaches ∞ is 0?
choices: −1/x ≤ sin(x)/x ≤ 1/x for x > 0, and both bounds tend to 0
items.explanation: Dividing −1 ≤ sin x ≤ 1 by x > 0 traps sin x / x between two bounds that both go to 0. The second option gives only an upper bound, which fixes no limit. The third is false because sin x has no limit at infinity.

items.prompt: The squeeze theorem is also known by which name?
items.explanation: The name sandwich theorem describes a function held between two bounds. The other names belong to different results in calculus.

items.prompt: Put the steps for finding the limit of x² · sin(1/x) as x approaches 0, in order.
steps: Multiply all three expressions by x², which keeps the inequalities because x² ≥ 0
Find that the limits of −x² and x² are both 0
Conclude that the limit of x² · sin(1/x) is 0
items.explanation: The bounds come first, then multiplying them by x², then the limits of the bounds, and last the conclusion drawn from the squeeze.

items.prompt: Which three conditions define the continuity of f at a?
choices: f(a) is defined, the limit at a exists, and the limit equals f(a)
f(a) is defined, f is positive, and f is increasing
The limit at a exists, f is a polynomial, and f(a) = 0
f has a derivative at a only
items.explanation: All three must hold together. Positivity and increase are not part of the definition, and a polynomial need not be zero at a.

items.prompt: Is f(x) = x² + 1 continuous at x = 2?
choices: No, because f is not a line
Yes, because the limit at 2 is 5 and f(2) is 5
Yes, because f(x) is always positive
items.explanation: The limit 5 equals f(2) = 5, so all three conditions hold. A function does not need to be linear to be continuous, and 2 being nonzero is irrelevant.

items.prompt: Let f(x) = (x² − 1)/(x − 1) for x ≠ 1, and f(1) = 5. Is f continuous at 1?
choices: No, the limit is 2 but f(1) = 5
No, the limit does not exist
items.explanation: Factoring gives x + 1 for x ≠ 1, so the limit is 2. Since f(1) = 5 differs, the third condition fails, and the break is removable. The limit does exist, so the last option is wrong.

items.prompt: Which function is NOT continuous at x = 2?
choices: f(x) = 1 for x < 2 and f(x) = 3 for x ≥ 2
items.explanation: The second function jumps from 1 to 3 at 2, so the one-sided limits differ. The others are continuous at 2 with values 8, 3 and 3/5.

items.prompt: What is true of every polynomial at every real number?
choices: It has a vertical asymptote there
It has a removable discontinuity there
items.explanation: Polynomials have no breaks, so they are continuous at every real number. The other options describe breaks, which polynomials do not have.

items.prompt: Which equation says f is continuous from the right at a?
choices: The right-hand limit of f at a equals f(a)
The limit of f at a equals 0
The right-hand limit at a equals the left-hand limit at a
The left-hand limit of f at a is infinite
items.explanation: Continuity from the right needs the right-hand limit to match the value at a. Equal one-sided limits describe whether the two-sided limit exists, and the other options are unrelated.

items.prompt: For f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2) when x ≠ 2, which value c for f(2) = c makes f continuous at 2?
items.explanation: Factoring gives x + 2 for x ≠ 2, so the limit is 4, and only c = 4 matches it. Choosing 2 confuses the point 2 with the limit.

items.prompt: The intermediate value theorem requires f to be continuous on what kind of set?
items.explanation: The theorem uses the values at both endpoints of a closed interval. A single point gives no values in between, and the integers and rationals are not intervals.

items.prompt: Suppose f is continuous on [1, 3], f(1) = −2, and f(3) = 4. What must be true?
choices: f(c) = 0 for some c between 1 and 3
items.explanation: 0 lies between −2 and 4, so the theorem guarantees a point c in [1, 3] with f(c) = 0. It does not say f(2) = 1, and f is not zero everywhere.

items.prompt: Let f(x) = x³ − x − 1 on [1, 2], where f(1) = −1 and f(2) = 5. What does the theorem give?
choices: A root in the open interval (1, 2)
Roots at both x = 1 and x = 2
items.explanation: f is a polynomial, so it is continuous, and it changes sign from −1 to 5. A root therefore lies in (1, 2). The claim f(1.5) = 0 is false, since f(1.5) = 0.875: the theorem gives a root without locating it.

items.prompt: Why does the theorem not guarantee a zero of f(x) = 1/x on [−1, 1], even though f(−1) < 0 < f(1)?
choices: f(−1) and f(1) are not whole numbers
f is not continuous on [−1, 1], since it is undefined at x = 0
The interval [−1, 1] has length 2, which is too long
items.explanation: The continuity hypothesis fails at x = 0, so the sign change does not force a zero. Indeed 1/x never equals 0. The whole-number option is irrelevant to the theorem's hypotheses.

items.prompt: Does the intermediate value theorem say how many roots a function has in an interval?
choices: At least one, but it does not say how many
items.explanation: The theorem guarantees at least one point with the target value. A function might have three roots in the interval, and the theorem would still hold.

items.prompt: Does f(x) = x − cos x have a root in (0, 1) by the intermediate value theorem?
choices: No, because cos x is never larger than x
items.explanation: f(0) = −1 and f(1) = 1 − cos 1, which is about 0.46 and positive. Since f is continuous, a root lies in (0, 1). The claim f(1) = 0 is false, because cos 1 is not 1.

items.prompt: Let f be continuous on [0, 4] with f(0) = 1 and f(4) = 7. Which conclusion is guaranteed?
choices: For every value between 1 and 7 there is a c in [0, 4] with f(c) equal to that value
f(c) = 1 for some c in the open interval (0, 4)
items.explanation: The theorem guarantees that every value between 1 and 7 is attained. The other options go beyond it: f need not be increasing, f(2) need not be 4, and f may equal 1 only at x = 0.

items.prompt: Put the steps of the bisection method for a continuous f on [a, b] with a sign change, in order.
steps: Check that f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs
Evaluate f at the midpoint c of [a, b]
Keep the half-interval where the sign still changes
Repeat with the smaller interval until it is small enough
items.explanation: The sign check must come first, because the theorem guarantees a root only when the sign changes. Each halving needs the midpoint value before a half can be chosen.
